newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservative contender Hague says no to EMU.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservative contender Hague says no to EMU.

text.p: Former Welsh secretary William Hague, one of the two frontrunners for the leadership of Britain's main opposition Conservative party, on Thursday ruled out joining the European Union's planned single currency.

"My policy would be, the policy in this parliament and the policy on which I would fight for the Conservative party to return to office at the next general election is that we would not abolish the pound," Hague said.
"As the leader of the party,I would be ruling out as our policy anything other than saying we are against economic and monetary union (EMU)," he told BBC radio.
Hague's comments were his clearest yet on the issue that has bitterly divided the party for several years and is dominating the leadership contest.
Hague's main challenger, ex-finance minister Kenneth Clarke, is a pro-European who believes Britain must keep its options open whether to join economic and monetary union (EMU) one day.
The other leadership contender, Euro-sceptic right-winger John Redwood, has ruled out ever scrapping the pound and his backers have accused Hague of being vague on the issue.
Hague said he had "principled objections" to EMU because of the economic risk and immense constitutional change it would entail.
He could not envisage at present abolishing the pound but added: "I'm not going to use the word never'."
Pressed to explain, he said: "I do not know in 30 or 40 years' time if we are dealing with a radically different Europe or a radically different proposition for a single currency.
"But I do know that the principled objections that I have to a single currency will hold good for a very long time to come."
Hague said this did not amount to a continuation of the Conservatives' current official wait and see' policy on EMU.
"The policy of our party very clearly would be that we would be opposed to economic and monetary union for principled reasons as well as because of the economic difficulties," he said.
